title: Millions spent in last two weeks before Maryland congressional primaries
summary: Late bursts of heavy spending in political primaries by outside groups is becoming more and more common, and nowhere is that more evident than in the 5th District House race, where almost $4 million has poured in since early June, mostly backing Del. Adrian Boafo.
content:
by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters June 20, 2026

by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters June 20, 2026

In just the last two weeks, almost $4 million has been poured into Maryland’s 5th District congressional race, mostly in support of Del. Adrian Boafo (D-Prince George’s).

Late bursts of heavy spending in political primaries is becoming more and more common, as political action committees continue to test boundaries, according to one political analyst. But in the 5th District, the flood of outside cash has not gone unnoticed by Boafo’s opponents in the crowded field of 24 Democrats.

The money since the last candidate reporting deadline on June 3 – $1.9 million from crypto super PAC Protect Progress, $1.5 million from AIPAC-affiliated United Democracy Project and $250,000 each from the PACs Project 218 and the Rolling Sea Action Fund – makes up a large part of the roughly $8.8 million spent by outside groups in support of Boafo’s campaign throughout the election cycle.

Three of Boafo’s opponents in the Democratic primary, former U.S. Capitol Police Officer Harry Dunn, businesswoman Quincy Bareebe and former Prince Georges County Executive Rushern Baker, recently came together to criticize the influx of cash on behalf of Boafo’s campaign. They called on him and his major endorsers to disavow the money and its influence.

In addition to financial support from outside groups, Boafo has also racked up an impressive list of endorsements from prominent Democrats, including Gov. Wes Moore, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and, most importantly, longtime Rep. Steny Hoyer, whose decision to step down after more than four decades in the House led to the Democratic scramble for the seat.

A Boafo campaign spokesman called the complaints by the other candidates a distraction and distortion.

“Unfortunately Adrian’s opponents have sunk to a new level of desperation in attacking Senator Alsobrooks, Governor Moore and Congressman Hoyer in their attempt to lie and mislead voters about Adrian’s record,” said Chris Taylor, spokesperson for Boafo’s campaign. “Adrian is focused on talking to voters about his vision for Maryland and will stand shoulder to shoulder with Angela, Wes and Steny fighting for Maryland families in Congress.”

Inside Elections Deputy Editor Jacob Rubashkin noted Boafo might be more insulated from these attacks than a less well-known candidate thanks to the endorsements of Hoyer, Alsobrooks and Moore.

“It’s not as if he’s a candidate who is relying entirely on financial support from outside groups to boost him,” Rubashkin said.

And regardless of how it benefited his campaign this cycle, the influence of outside money has been a focal point of Boafo’s own campaign platform. Listed at the top of his democracy and civil rights agenda, one goal on Boafo’s website is to “Overturn Citizens United and reduce the influence of unlimited corporate money in our elections.” Citizens United is the 2010 Supreme Court decision that equated political spending with free speech, essentially opening the floodgates to heavy campaign spending by special interest groups.

A product of that influence, late bursts of heavy spending like that in District 5, are becoming more and more common in congressional primaries, Rubashkin said. That wasn’t so much the case as recently as three election cycles ago, he said.

“This is all kind of a 2022 and onwards development,” he said. “We’re still relatively early in the … post-Citizens United era.”

Protect Progress, for example, was only registered with the Federal Election Commission in August 2023, and the United Democracy Project registered in January 2022.

“Every cycle, super PACs grow more numerous, and donors get more comfortable spending more amounts of money in primaries,” Rubashkin said. “That didn’t used to happen. And every year, there are going to be political actors who push the envelope a little further, see what they can get away with.”

Donors and PACs have been able to get away with more while the FEC has been short of the six commissioners normally heading the body, Rubashkin said. In order to have a quorum, at least four commissioners are needed.

That quorum was last lost shortly after the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump ousted FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub, a Democrat, and only two commissioners were left by April that year. Though Trump nominated two Republican replacements in February this year, they haven’t been confirmed by the Senate.

Without a quorum, the FEC has been unable to make decisions such as issuing rules or legal guidance, holding public meetings and fining violators of campaign finance laws. Rubashkin said that a full FEC is “the first step” in the process of getting big outside money out of elections.

One way PACs have been getting around FEC regulations nationally has been through “pop-up PACs,” that are registered on a specific time frame so they’re then able to spend money on a later election without disclosing their donors or other information until after the election. Politico reported Sunday that across the country, these groups have made up 1 in 10 dollars of outside spending for congressional primaries this year.

There’s nothing stopping Congress from closing that loophole statutorily, according to Rubashkin. More difficult would be instituting a constitutional amendment that could overturn the decision of Citizens United.

“But otherwise, I think things will get worse before they get better,” he said.
